title: Same Average, Six Very Different Weeks
scopeNote: This keeps the daily simulation and the event delivery that makes contingency and recovery visible, cut to three people and two domains, each deliverable once on a fixed day. A fourth person, choosing when events land, positive as well as negative events, and a wider set of domains stay in the longer version.
summary: Three fictional people with identical average self-esteem and identical-looking weeks. Deliver one setback and how much they move, what moves them and how long it lasts come apart.
learningObjectives: Separate level, day-to-day variability, contingency and recovery.
Explain why a single score estimates only the first of those.
Explain why how much somebody moves ordinarily does not predict what knocks them over.
Explain why being strongly affected by one kind of event is not general fragility.
Recognise recovery as a third property implied by neither of the others.
Treat variability as a characteristic rather than a symptom.
interactionTypes: a prediction about what one score tells you
six weeks of daily readings for three people
events the learner delivers to all three at once
a summary table separating four properties a single score collapses
a comparison between two domains that affect the three people differently
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. The learner is asked nothing about themselves, no questionnaire is offered and no score is produced for anybody.
dataStatus: Three invented people on an arbitrary scale, with days produced by a formula from a fixed random seed. Low or variable values here are characteristics that differ between people, not symptoms, and nothing on the page is a clinical statement or a basis for interpreting anyone's wellbeing.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. Events are ordinary buttons, and a delivered one is marked with aria-disabled rather than the disabled attribute so it stays reachable and readable. All four properties are in a real table with row and column headers, so the figure is never the only route to them, and a person who has not recovered is described in words rather than by an absent value. Each line is labelled by name at its end, event markers are labelled with what was delivered, and the chart description gives every average and every day-to-day movement. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
simulationNotes: A day's state is a baseline plus the accumulated effect of delivered events, each decaying by half every recovery-period days, plus ordinary day-to-day movement of a person-specific size. The three people share a baseline and differ on the other three parameters, which are arranged so that the properties are visibly separate rather than three names for one thing. Cleo is as steady as Ada with nothing happening and is the only one for whom a setback at work is a catastrophe, so variability and contingency cannot be the same property; she is also the least affected of the three by a falling-out with a friend, so being strongly contingent is not general fragility; and Ada is back within days where Cleo has not returned by the end of the six weeks, so recovery is implied by neither of the others. Each person's daily fluctuations are drawn once from a fixed seed and centred to mean zero, so that with nothing delivered all three six-week averages are exactly the baseline; the activity opens by claiming the three scored identically, and an average of 61.4 against 62.3 would undercut the claim on the first screen. Day-to-day movement is always computed on the event-free series, so an event's effect is never counted as volatility. Simplifications, all stated: events arrive when a button is pressed rather than partly in consequence of how somebody is already doing, which is the largest thing this cannot represent; recovery is a smooth decay back to exactly the starting point; the two domains are invented labels rather than a taxonomy; and nothing anybody does changes their own contingencies.
readmeTopic: the four things a single self-esteem score collapses into one
